abstract: This report from Anthropic analyzes AI's economic impact through novel 'economic primitives'—foundational measures of how Claude is used across five dimensions: task complexity, human and AI skills, use case type, AI autonomy, and task success. Analyzing 1 million Claude.ai and 1 million API conversations from November 2025, the study finds that 49% of jobs now use AI for at least 25% of tasks (up from 36% in early 2025), with widespread adoption potentially boosting US labor productivity by 1.0-1.8 percentage points annually, though success rates and regional variation significantly affect these estimates.
keyFindings: 49% of jobs now use AI for at least 25% of their tasks, up from 36% in early 2025, with potential productivity gains of 1.0-1.8 percentage points annually
Claude usage has become more evenly distributed across US states (Gini coefficient fell from 0.37 to 0.32 in 3 months), suggesting convergence to usage parity within 2-5 years at current rates

Task success rates vary substantially by complexity: Claude succeeds at harder tasks less often, and adjusting productivity estimates for reliability roughly halves implied gains from 1.8 to 1.0 percentage points annually

Geographic variation is pronounced: work use is highest in higher-income countries (60%+) while coursework use dominates lower-income countries; GDP per capita explains global variation with 0.7% increase in usage per 1% GDP increase
Claude tends to handle higher-education tasks disproportionately, creating a net deskilling effect across most occupations as AI removes more skilled components of jobs rather than routine work
methodology: Privacy-preserving analysis of two random samples from November 13-20, 2025: 1 million Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro, Max tiers) and 1 million first-party API transcripts. Economic primitives were operationalized by prompting Claude to classify anonymized conversations along five dimensions. Task-level data from O*NET; geographic analysis used IP geolocation (ISO-3166 codes) and World Bank population data. Validation compared classifiers against human ratings on small permitted samples and external benchmarks (BLS educational attainment data, productivity study correlations). Diffusion modeling used ordinary least squares, weighted least squares, and two-stage least squares regression with workforce composition as instrument.
qualifiers: Analysis based on three months of data only; diffusion estimates carry high uncertainty and may not sustain; economic primitives are directionally accurate but individually 'noisy' and not definitive (e.g., may underestimate human education requirements); results exclude conversations flagged for trust/safety violations and exclude users on VPNs or hosting services; US state-level analyses excluded Wyoming due to abusive traffic; global analyses filtered cells with fewer than 15 conversations and 5 unique accounts; API data limited to single input-output pairs rather than full conversation trajectories; productivity estimates reflect current model capabilities which are rapidly advancing; relationships between primitives differ between country and state levels without clear causal interpretation.
